title: Banks, super funds to face AI stress test
full_text:
The country's largest banks, pension funds and insurers will be stress-tested for their resilience to artificial intelligence-driven threats, as well as extreme market volatility, with the prudential regulator warning many firms are ill-prepared for the growing risks posed by AI.
The first-of-its-kind test, to be conducted by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority next year, will examine how the financial system responds to potential AI-led disruption.
APRA boss John Lonsdale said major institutions were "not where they needed to be" on AI and had failed to keep pace with increasing threats since it first put the industry on notice in April.
"The second big element that we're very concerned about is the use of AI for threat," Lonsdale said. "There are very large amounts of resources being invested by entities to essentially plug holes in legacy systems.
"The speed with which AI can be used to identify issues and vulnerabilities and cause problems is something that we're very concerned about."
APRA's letter in April warned boards were not yet technically literate on AI and its emerging risks, arguing they were over-reliant on vendor presentations that did not consider risks such as unpredictable model behaviour or cyber breaches.
Lonsdale said the landscape had evolved rapidly over the past six months, including several instances of AI exploiting vulnerabilities with or without any explicit direction. Quantum computing could also render existing defences ineffective, APRA said in its system risk report.
In one high-profile example, an OpenAI agent autonomously broke through defences designed to protect certain non-public Medicare data and other government information. Instead of immediately disclosing the breach, the company informed the government months after the fact.
Lonsdale said this was one of many incidents APRA was examining to figure out how the financial sector could improve, with the regulator set to put AI front and centre of its 2027 system-wide stress test.
"The exercise will look at risks that could emerge in severe but plausible downside scenarios, either from rapid AI adoption disrupting some business models, or a sharp downward reassessment of AI-related asset valuation," APRA said on Thursday.
Lonsdale confirmed that 2027 would be the first time the test would explicitly consider an AI-created threat - an area that has increasingly occupied the regulator as it tries to protect the stability of the Australian financial system.
At The Australian Financial Review Super and Wealth Summit last month, APRA deputy chairman David Bradbury said an AI attack on the $4.8 trillion super industry "could actually start to clean out people's accounts".
Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said in its 2026 global threat report that AI-enabled cyberattacks had doubled year-on-year.
"More sophisticated threat actors will highly likely successfully leverage AI for malware development, social engineering, and post-exploitation activities, accelerating their operational tempo and attack effectiveness at scales previously unattainable," the report said.
Lonsdale said APRA was particularly concerned about third-party suppliers that could transmit threats to a broader range of institutions.
The regulator said the financial system remained resilient despite these risks.
